« Ça fait des années qu’on le dit » – À: “We’ve been saying it for years”: In Montréal-Nord, the Station 39 scandal surprises no one
À Montréal-Nord, les allégations visant: In Montréal-Nord, allegations against 16 police officers are reviving complaints of racial profiling and a crisis of trust.
‍<strong>Pour plusieurs résidents de Mon: ‍For many residents of Montréal-Nord, the revelations about 16 officers at Neighbourhood Station 39 didn’t come as a surprise so much as a feeling of déjà vu. Residents, community organizations and outreach workers describe experiences they say they have been denouncing for years. We spoke with those who say they live with the consequences of racial profiling and those trying to repair the damage.
Appuyée sur une béquille, le regard rivé: Leaning on a crutch, her eyes fixed on the crowd ahead, Karen presses forward on rue Langelier to catch up with the protest. It’s around 8:30 p.m., and the protesters, who first gathered in front of Neighbourhood Station 39 (PDQ 39) in Montréal-Nord, have decided to march through the streets of the neighbourhood, shouting their anger and outrage over the allegations against officers at the station.
La résidente du boulevard Lacordaire aur: The boulevard Lacordaire resident could have stayed home, but as soon as she heard about the protest, she took to the streets. “I had to be here,” says the Quebecer of Mexican origin, straining to quicken her pace alongside her daughter and her partner. Karen joined the march despite her difficulty getting around because she says she recognizes in this affair part of what her own son is going through.
Âgé de 17 ans et étudiant à l’école seco: The 17-year-old, a student at École secondaire Henri-Bourassa, has allegedly been targeted repeatedly by police officers in the neighbourhood. “Every time he’s with his friends, it’s the same officers following him, stopping him, pinning him to the ground,” she says. On her phone, she shows videos and photos she has been keeping for months. Some of the images show marks left by handcuffs.
Dans l’une des interventions qui l’ont p: In one incident that particularly shook her, her son was brought home by officers who suspected him of stealing a vehicle. “I asked them, ‘If he stole a car, why are you bringing him home?’ They laughed at me,” she recalls, indignant.
Quarante-huit heures après les révélatio: Forty-eight hours after Fady Dagher’s shocking revelations, people in Montréal-Nord are speaking out (again) to describe everyday scenes like those experienced by Karen and her son. And here, no one says they’re surprised by what Montréal’s police chief appears to be discovering.
Karen n’est pas le seul visage de cette: Karen isn’t the only face of this anger. Further along, Mahmoud Canly is also taking part in the protest. The Quebecer of Kurdish origin says he’s there because he recognizes in the current revelations an experience that deeply affected his family.
À l’été 2023, des policiers sont interve: In the summer of 2023, police officers came to his home after a report about his youngest daughter’s screaming. When Mahmoud arrived after work, several police cars were parked in front of the house. His wife and teenage son had been separated to be questioned.
Trois ans plus tard, il affirme que les: Three years later, he says the physical and psychological scars are still there. “My wife isn’t doing any better psychologically. She’s still hurting. Every time she saw the living room of our old house, it reminded her of what happened.” The couple eventually sold their home and moved to another part of Montréal-Nord. “We changed houses just to have some peace,” he says.
La famille a porté plainte et entrepris: The family filed a complaint and took various steps, but Mahmoud feels he never got satisfactory answers. “They denied what happened. That hurts even more […] They’re stronger.”
Il explique que, s’il participe aujourd’: He explains that he is taking part in the press conference and the march today because he doesn’t want other families to go through the same thing. “It has to stop. We live in a civilized society. I know there are good police officers. Those who see things have to have the courage to speak out.”
<strong>« Nous sommes indignés, mais mal: “We are outraged, but unfortunately not surprised”
Quelques heures avant la manifestation,: A few hours before the protest, representatives of the Regroupement des intervenants et intervenantes d’origine haïtienne (RIIOH) gathered at the offices of the Café-Jeunesse Multiculturel on rue Pascal. The group had come to respond to revelations that 16 officers from PDQ 39 are facing administrative measures following allegations of racist remarks and behaviour targeting, among others, Black and Arab people.
Dans son communiqué, le RIIOH parle de r: In its press release, the RIIOH describes the revelations as “serious, revolting and unacceptable,” saying they confirm what residents, families, young people and organizations have been denouncing for years: the existence of discriminatory behaviour and practices that penalize many Black and Arab residents. Accounts of racial profiling, discrimination and differential treatment have too often been minimized, questioned or ignored, according to the group. “Today, we are outraged, but unfortunately not surprised,” says the group’s spokesperson, Sheila Fortuné.
Pour le RIIOH, l’enjeu dépasse largement: For the RIIOH, the issue goes far beyond the officers involved. The group refuses to let the affair be reduced to the actions of a few individuals and believes it raises systemic questions of governance, accountability and trust between institutions and communities.
Vendredi dernier, le directeur du Servic: Last Friday, the director of the Service de police de la Ville de Montréal (SPVM), Fady Dagher, announced that 2 officers had been suspended and 14 other members of PDQ 39 removed from active duty. The internal investigation was launched after officers at the station themselves reported behaviour deemed unacceptable within their unit.
Les révélations ont rapidement provoqué: The revelations quickly sent shock waves. The Ligue des droits et libertés is calling for a public inquiry into racism within the SPVM, as well as an end to police street checks.
La mairesse de l’arrondissement de Montr: Montréal-Nord borough mayor Christine Black said the revelations had reopened “wounds and experiences that go back a long way” for many residents, particularly within Black, Arab and racialized communities. “Any form of racism, discrimination or racial profiling is unacceptable,” she added, saying institutions had “not yet done enough to stem racism.”
La nouvelle mairesse de Montréal, Soraya: Montréal’s new mayor, Soraya Martinez Ferrada, also acknowledged the existence of systemic racism. “I want to speak to the residents of Montréal-Nord, to everyone who has ever felt watched, targeted, profiled […] We live in a society where systemic racism exists,” she said.
À Québec, la première ministre Christine: In Quebec City, Premier Christine Fréchette called for the affair to be fully and quickly brought to light, while Public Security Minister Ian Lafrenière described the allegations as “completely unacceptable and shocking.”
Samuel Bunche n’a pas besoin de réfléchi: Samuel Bunche doesn’t have to think long when asked whether he has ever experienced racial profiling. “A ton,” he answers. The 30-year-old Montréal-Nord resident says he grew up in the neighbourhood. A martial arts athlete involved in several community activities, he estimates he has been stopped by police “about a hundred times” in his life. “I’ve been arrested a lot, put in police cars, stopped. I’d say at least a hundred times,” he tells La Converse.
Il évoque plusieurs interventions qui, s: He describes several incidents that he believes amounted to racial profiling. One of them, in Laval, led to a civil lawsuit. After three years of proceedings, the City of Laval acknowledged racial profiling in his case and paid him compensation. But that isn’t the episode that affected him the most. What worries him more, he says, is how normalized these experiences have become. “There are so many situations happening that it becomes normal. That’s the problem. It happens so often that we’re exhausted. We tell ourselves, ‘It’s going to happen again tomorrow, again next week.’”
Selon lui, cette résignation est largeme: According to him, this resignation is widely shared in the neighbourhood. “Every day, we hear stories. Nothing surprises us anymore. It happens so much that it doesn’t surprise us anymore.” So the revelations about PDQ 39 didn’t surprise him. “What’s surprising is the way it came out and the fact that they’re acknowledging it. Because it’s often been denied.” Over the years, these experiences have also taken a more personal toll. Samuel says he feels a kind of anxiety every time he comes across police officers. “When I see the police, I ask myself, ‘Did I do something wrong? Is this about me?’” It’s a reaction he considers abnormal. “I’m not a stressed-out person in life. But when I see the police, I start questioning myself and I feel this anxiety rising. That shouldn’t be normal. I shouldn’t feel that when I see the police.”
Pour comprendre pourquoi les révélations: To understand why the revelations about PDQ 39 are sparking more anger than surprise in Montréal-Nord, you have to walk through the doors of community organizations. It’s at the Café-Jeunesse Multiculturel, where the RIIOH held its press conference, that Slim Hammami welcomes young people from the neighbourhood every day. For the organization’s director, the scandal is no revelation. “We were surprised,” he says, “by the scale, by the number of officers involved and by the measures announced. But by the conduct itself, no. It’s been going on for years in Montréal-Nord.”
Les récits d’interventions policières fo: Accounts of police interventions are part of the organization’s daily life. “The vast majority of the young people we see have stories with the police. We support them, we listen to them. Stories, we have plenty of them,” says Hammami. In his view, what’s really new is that this behaviour is now being publicly acknowledged: “Maybe what happened will wake some people up.”
Si plusieurs évoquent le souvenir des ém: While many recall the 2008 riots that followed the death of Fredy Villanueva, Slim Hammami doesn’t believe a similar scenario will unfold, noting that the young man’s death served as a trigger after years of built-up tensions.
Dix-huit ans plus tard, il craint toutef: Eighteen years later, however, he fears that promises of change will meet the same fate as they did after 2008. “We played the game. We collaborated. We created spaces for discussion. Then things were kind of forgotten,” he laments to La Converse.
Pour lui, la stigmatisation persistante: For him, the persistent stigmatization of Montréal-Nord and its crime problems are sometimes used to justify certain police behaviour. “We have to remember one simple thing: Montréal-Nord is a place where the rule of law applies, and police officers have to do their job properly.”
Le RIIOH souhaite maintenant rencontrer: The RIIOH now wants to meet with SPVM director Fady Dagher. “We are deeply rooted in the neighbourhood. We hope to be heard and that the discussions will start from what people are actually living on the ground.”
À Montréal-Nord, une autre question revi: In Montréal-Nord, another question keeps coming up in conversations: how can so many residents say they have had similar experiences for years?
Pour Salim Baghdadi, sociologue et coord: For Salim Baghdadi, a sociologist and urban safety coordinator at the Table de quartier de Montréal-Nord, the neighbourhood’s reaction is not surprising. “For years, young people, families and residents have been describing certain experiences. Organizations and outreach workers have been hearing them for a long time,” he says.
Selon lui, chaque intervention policière: According to him, each police intervention is generally examined as an isolated event. But when similar accounts pile up over years, they paint a broader picture. “An individual experience can always be interpreted in different ways. But when several people who don’t know each other describe comparable situations, it becomes a social phenomenon that must be taken seriously.”
Sans se prononcer sur les enquêtes en co: Without commenting on the ongoing investigations, the sociologist is already seeing the consequences of this accumulation of accounts, because, he notes, “when part of the population feels it will not be treated the same way as other citizens, trust in institutions gradually erodes.”
Cette méfiance touche aussi les mécanism: This distrust also extends to complaint mechanisms: “Many people tell us they don’t see the point of filing a complaint because they feel it won’t change anything.” For Salim Baghdadi, the PDQ 39 affair therefore goes beyond individual responsibility and raises the question of the relationship between a public institution and part of the population it is supposed to serve.
Il souligne toutefois un élément porteur: He does, however, point to a hopeful sign: the reports that led to the investigation came from police officers themselves, and “that shows that within the institution itself, some people refused to stay silent.” It remains to be seen whether this reckoning will help rebuild trust that has long been fragile.
<strong>Une marche vers un souvenir impo: A march toward a memory that cannot be forgotten
Vers 22 h, les manifestants arrivent dev: Around 10 p.m., the protesters arrive at Henri-Bourassa Park, where Fredy Villanueva was killed by a police officer in August 2008. Eighteen years later, his name still comes up in conversation whenever relations between the police and the neighbourhood resurface.
Pour plusieurs participants, la destinat: For many participants, the march’s destination is highly symbolic, a reminder that the current debates are part of a much longer history. A history of distrust, wounds and promises of change.
Aujourd’hui, les organismes communautair: Today, community organizations see the PDQ 39 revelations as an opportunity to reopen a discussion they have long considered necessary. What remains to be seen, they say, is whether this time the residents of Montréal-Nord will truly feel heard.
Montréal-Nord secouée par des allégation: Montréal-Nord shaken by allegations of racial profiling at PDQ 39 as residents march to express anger and distrust toward police
Montréal-Nord est au cœur d’une controve: Montréal-Nord is at the centre of a controversy after allegations of racist remarks and behaviour against 16 officers at PDQ 39. A citizens’ march brought together residents to denounce racial profiling and voice their anger over experiences they say they have endured for years, while community organizations and elected officials call for change and a thorough investigation into police practices.
